To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

panic disorder is a heterogeneous condition with two distinct subtypes, a respiratory subtype and a somatic subtype, which are associated with different risk factors, different clinical course and different response to pharmacotherapy.
the best fit for the data is a two class model for all samples.

1) panic disorder is a heterogeneous syndrome with two subtypes that can be distinguished by the presence of respiratory versus general somatic symptoms, 2) these subtypes are present in both epidemiological and clinical samples, and 3) they appear to be present in both the United States and Germany.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of clinically meaningful phenotypic variants of panic disorder and their implications for the etiopathophysiology of panic disorder.
identifying clinically relevant and potentially etiologically meaningful phenotypes of panic disorder (PD) and panic symptoms.
identifying the most appropriate model for the structure of panic symptoms, and with using that model to identify the most appropriate subgroups within the larger population of patients with PD.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the evidence supports the existence of two major phenotypes, one of which is a respiratory subtype.
there is evidence for two subtypes of PD, one characterized by respiratory and the other by somatic panic symptoms.
panic disorder and its sub-types have not been identified and the heterogeneity of panic is still a matter for debate.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the respiratory component of panic attacks appears to be a relatively stable and consistent feature of PD.
panic is a heterogeneous syndrome with at least two distinct phenotypes, with one characterized by respiratory symptoms and a second characterized by general somatic complaints.
there is a respiratory subtype of panic that is distinct from other subtypes of panic.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there is a respiratory variant of panic disorder, which is more common than the more traditional non-respiratory form.
panic is not one disorder but rather several distinct subtypes.
the heterogeneity of PD is real and should be considered when planning clinical trials.
